subsection: 2. Human interaction with the rock cycle

notes.b: Humans interact with the rock cycle by extracting rock, minerals and energy from the crust.
points: Extraction removes rock far faster than natural weathering and erosion, and it exposes fresh rock to weathering.
Extraction creates new deposits of waste, which are stored on the surface.
People act as an exogenic process: removing rock is the human equivalent of erosion, and dumping waste is the human equivalent of deposition.

notes.h: Mining: what is mined and how it is worked
notes.b: Mining removes metal ores, coal and salt from the crust.
points: Mined materials include metal ores (zinc, lead, copper, gold), coal and salt.
Ore bodies form where minerals are concentrated by igneous activity or by hot fluids moving through rock.
Exploration uses geological surveys and test drilling before a mine is developed.
Open-cast (open-pit) mining removes the overburden and works ore that lies near the surface.
Underground (shaft) mining reaches deep ore through shafts and tunnels; room and pillar is one underground method.
Processing crushes and grinds the ore and separates the mineral from the waste rock.
Waste rock is stored in spoil heaps, and fine waste, called tailings, is stored in tailings ponds.

Tara Mines, Navan, Co. Meath: an underground zinc and lead mine, Europe's largest zinc mine, in production since 1977 and owned by the Swedish company Boliden; the ore lies in Carboniferous limestone.
Bingham Canyon copper mine, Utah, USA: one of the largest open-pit mines in the world.
Super Pit gold mine, Kalgoorlie, Western Australia: a large open-pit gold mine.

Aberfan, south Wales, 21 October 1966: a colliery spoil tip built over springs on a hillside collapsed into the village after heavy rain, burying Pantglas Junior School; 144 people were killed, 116 of them children.
Aberfan was a flow slide of saturated waste, a mass movement process.
Landscape scars and subsidence occur above and around underground workings.
Spoil heaps and tailings take up land.
Avoca, Co. Wicklow: centuries of copper mining, now closed, left acid mine drainage that discolours and pollutes the Avoca River with heavy metals.
Dust, noise and heavy traffic affect people living near the mine.
Positive impacts are jobs, exports and local spending.
Environmental licensing and monitoring control the handling of waste and the quality of water leaving the site.
Tailings ponds are lined to stop seepage and capped when they are closed.
Lisheen, Co. Tipperary: a zinc and lead mine that closed in 2015; the site was rehabilitated.

notes.b: Quarries work rock and sand close to the surface for cement, aggregate, building stone and roofing.
points: Limestone is quarried for cement, aggregate and lime for agriculture.
Sand and gravel come from glacial and fluvio-glacial deposits and are used in concrete.
Granite and other dimension stone are cut from the rock for building.
Slate is quarried for roofing, and marble for decoration.
1. Remove the overburden: the soil and glacial till above the rock.
2. Cut benches into the rock face.
3. Drill and blast the rock.
4. Crush and screen the rock, grading it by size.
Dimension stone is cut to size rather than blasted.
Limestone is crushed and mixed with shale, then heated in a kiln to make clinker; the clinker is ground with gypsum to make cement.
Heating limestone releases carbon dioxide, because calcium carbonate gives lime and carbon dioxide.
The carbon dioxide returns to the atmosphere carbon that had been locked in the rock for hundreds of millions of years.
Irish Cement's works at Platin, near Drogheda, Co. Meath, and at Castlemungret, Co. Limerick, are both based on Carboniferous limestone.
Sand and gravel: large pits in glacial deposits around Blessington, Co. Wicklow.
Granite: quarried at Ballyknockan, Co. Wicklow, from the Leinster granite.
Marble: green Connemara marble is quarried in Connemara, Co. Galway.
Slate: quarried on Valentia Island, Co. Kerry.
Permanent scars, and loss of farmland and habitat.
Dust, noise and blasting vibration, and heavy lorries on rural roads.
Lowering of the local water table.
Positive impacts are jobs and the materials needed for housing and roads.
Planning permission comes with conditions on working hours, and limits on dust and noise.
Earth banks and trees screen the quarry from view.
Worked-out quarries are rehabilitated as lakes, wildlife habitats, landfill or amenity areas.

notes.h: How oil and gas form and are trapped
points: The remains of tiny marine organisms are buried in sea-floor sediment.
Heat and pressure over millions of years turn these remains into oil and gas.
Oil and gas migrate upward through porous, permeable reservoir rock, such as sandstone.
They are trapped beneath impermeable cap rock, such as shale, in an anticline, a fault or a salt dome.

notes.h: Oil and gas exploitation and Irish fields
points: Seismic surveys locate possible traps, and exploratory wells test them.
Production uses production platforms or subsea wells, with pipelines to an onshore terminal.
Kinsale Head gas field, off the Co. Cork coast: discovered 1971, in production from 1978; Ireland's first commercial gas field; production ended in 2020 when the field was depleted.

Corrib gas field, off the coast of north-west Co. Mayo: discovered 1996, and gas first flowed in December 2015; gas is piped ashore to a processing terminal at Bellanaboy, Co. Mayo, originally operated by Shell.

Opposition at Corrib: the Shell to Sea campaign objected to a high-pressure raw-gas pipeline near homes, and five local men, the Rossport Five, were jailed in 2005 for refusing to obey a court order not to obstruct the pipeline work.

notes.h: Oil spills and the North Sea
points: The Deepwater Horizon oil rig, leased by BP in the Gulf of Mexico, exploded on 20 April 2010, killing 11 workers.
About 4.9 million barrels of oil spilled before the well was sealed.
The spill damaged fishing, tourism and wildlife along the US Gulf coast.
The North Sea, shared by the UK and Norway, is a major oil and gas province.

notes.h: Fracking and the impacts of oil and gas
points: Hydraulic fracturing (fracking) of shale releases gas; concerns include groundwater pollution and induced earthquakes.
Ireland banned onshore fracking by law in 2017.
Positive impacts are energy supply and security, revenue and jobs.
Negative impacts are oil spills, damage to marine life and fishing, and conflict with local communities.
Burning fossil fuels returns stored carbon to the atmosphere, contributing to climate change.
Heat comes from the earth's interior, from radioactive decay and residual heat.
Temperature rises with depth at about 25 to 30 °C per kilometre; this is the geothermal gradient.
Heat is greatest near plate boundaries and hotspots, where magma lies close to the surface.
Groundwater is heated by hot rock near magma.
Production wells bring steam and hot water to the surface.
Steam drives turbines to generate electricity, and hot water heats buildings through district heating.
Cooled water is pumped back down a reinjection well.
Ground-source heat pumps use the steady warmth of shallow ground to heat homes.
Enhanced geothermal systems pump water into hot dry rock to fracture it, so that the water picks up heat.

notes.h: Geothermal in Iceland and other countries
points: Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge above a hotspot, which gives it geothermal heat.
About 9 out of 10 homes in Iceland are heated by geothermal water.
Geothermal power provides between a quarter and a third of Iceland's electricity; most of the rest is hydro.
Hellisheiði is Iceland's largest geothermal power station, and Reykjavík has a geothermal district heating system.
The Blue Lagoon is a pool of warm, mineral-rich waste water from the Svartsengi power station, now a tourist attraction.
Larderello, Tuscany, Italy: the world's first geothermal electricity (1904) and first commercial geothermal power station (1913).
Wairakei, New Zealand: geothermal power station opened in 1958.
Ireland is far from a plate boundary, so it has only low-temperature geothermal potential.
Warm springs at Mallow, Co. Cork, show that heated groundwater exists.
Ground-source heat pumps are the main use.

notes.h: Advantages and disadvantages of geothermal energy
points: Advantages: renewable, low carbon emissions, reliable because it does not depend on the weather, and cheap to run once built.
Disadvantages: it is limited to suitable locations, and drilling costs are high.
Hydrogen sulphide gas is released, giving a rotten-egg smell.
Minerals are deposited in pipes as the hot water cools.
Basel, Switzerland: an enhanced geothermal project triggered small earthquakes in 2006 and was abandoned.

keyTerms.definition: The soil and glacial till lying above rock that must be removed before it is quarried or mined.
Mining of ore near the surface by removing the overburden to form an open pit.
The fine waste left after ore has been crushed and the mineral separated, stored in tailings ponds.
Acidic water draining from mine workings and waste, which carries heavy metals into rivers.
The material produced when crushed limestone and shale are heated in a kiln, ground with gypsum to make cement.
Porous, permeable rock in which oil and gas collect after migrating upward.
Impermeable rock, such as shale, that traps oil and gas beneath it.
Hydraulic fracturing: forcing fluid into shale at high pressure to fracture it and release gas.
The rise in temperature with depth, averaging about 25 to 30 °C per kilometre.
A device that draws the steady warmth of shallow ground to heat a building.
A well through which cooled geothermal water is pumped back underground.
A small earthquake triggered by human activity, such as fluid injection into rock.

factCards.term: Human interaction with the rock cycle: three ways extraction changes it
factCards.definition: It removes rock far faster than natural weathering and erosion; it exposes fresh rock to weathering; it creates new deposits of waste on the surface. Removal is the human equivalent of erosion, dumping the equivalent of deposition.

factCards.term: Mining: how ore bodies form, and Tara Mines as an Irish example
factCards.definition: Ore bodies form where igneous activity or hot fluids moving through rock concentrate minerals. Tara Mines, Navan, Co. Meath: underground zinc and lead mine in Carboniferous limestone; Europe's largest zinc mine; opened in 1977; owned by Swedish firm Boliden.

factCards.term: Mining: the stages from exploration to waste disposal
factCards.definition: Surveys and test drilling find the ore; open-cast mining strips the overburden to reach shallow ore (e.g. Bingham Canyon copper mine, Utah); underground mining uses shafts and tunnels; ore is crushed and separated; waste goes to spoil heaps and tailings ponds.

factCards.term: Aberfan disaster, 1966: what happened
factCards.definition: On 21 October 1966 a colliery spoil tip built over springs on a hillside above Aberfan, south Wales, collapsed after heavy rain as a flow slide of saturated waste, burying Pantglas Junior School; 144 people were killed, 116 of them children.

factCards.term: Mining: four negative impacts and three positive ones
factCards.definition: Landscape scars and subsidence; spoil heaps and tailings taking up land; acid mine drainage and heavy-metal pollution, as copper mining left in the Avoca River, Co. Wicklow; dust, noise and heavy traffic. Positive: jobs, exports and local spending.

factCards.term: Mining: how its impacts are managed, with an Irish example
factCards.definition: Environmental licensing and monitoring of waste and water leaving the site; lining tailings ponds to stop seepage and capping them at closure; rehabilitation after closure, as at Lisheen, Co. Tipperary, a zinc and lead mine that closed in 2015.

factCards.term: Quarrying: five materials and what each is used for
factCards.definition: Limestone: cement, aggregate and agricultural lime. Sand and gravel from glacial and fluvio-glacial deposits: concrete. Granite and other dimension stone: building, kerbs, headstones. Slate: roofing. Marble: decoration.

factCards.term: Quarrying: the stages of working a quarry
factCards.definition: First, the overburden of soil and glacial till is removed; then benches are cut into the rock face; the rock is drilled and blasted; finally it is crushed and screened (graded by size). Dimension stone is cut rather than blasted.

factCards.term: Cement: how it is made and why it releases carbon dioxide
factCards.definition: Limestone is crushed, mixed with shale and heated in a kiln to make clinker, which is ground with gypsum. Heating turns calcium carbonate into lime and carbon dioxide, returning to the air carbon locked in rock for hundreds of millions of years.

factCards.term: Name an Irish quarry site for cement, sand and gravel, granite, marble and slate
factCards.definition: Cement: Irish Cement at Platin, near Drogheda, Co. Meath, and Castlemungret, Co. Limerick (Carboniferous limestone). Sand and gravel: Blessington, Co. Wicklow. Granite: Ballyknockan, Co. Wicklow. Marble: Connemara. Slate: Valentia Island, Co. Kerry.

factCards.term: Quarrying: five negative impacts and two positive ones
factCards.definition: Permanent scars; loss of farmland and habitat; dust, noise and blasting vibration; heavy lorries on rural roads; a lowered local water table. Positive: jobs, and the materials needed for housing and roads.

factCards.term: Quarrying: how its impacts are managed
factCards.definition: Planning permission with conditions on working hours and limits on dust and noise; earth banks and trees to screen the quarry; rehabilitation of worked-out quarries as lakes, wildlife habitats, landfill or amenity areas.

factCards.term: Oil and gas: how they form and become trapped
factCards.definition: Remains of tiny marine organisms are buried in sea-floor sediment; over millions of years heat and pressure make oil and gas, which rise through porous, permeable reservoir rock (e.g. sandstone) until trapped under cap rock in an anticline, fault or salt dome.

factCards.term: Oil and gas: the stages of exploitation
factCards.definition: Seismic surveys locate possible traps; exploratory wells test them; production platforms or subsea wells bring up the oil or gas; pipelines carry it to an onshore terminal.

factCards.term: Kinsale Head and Corrib gas fields: locations and key dates
factCards.definition: Kinsale Head, off Co. Cork: discovered 1971, produced from 1978 until depleted in 2020; Ireland's first commercial gas field. Corrib, off north-west Co. Mayo: discovered 1996, first gas December 2015, piped to Bellanaboy terminal, originally run by Shell.

factCards.term: Corrib gas: why local people opposed it
factCards.definition: The Shell to Sea campaign objected to a high-pressure raw-gas pipeline near homes. In 2005 five local men, the Rossport Five, were jailed for refusing to obey a court order not to obstruct the pipeline work.

factCards.term: Deepwater Horizon: what happened and its effects
factCards.definition: The oil rig, leased by BP in the Gulf of Mexico, exploded on 20 April 2010, killing 11 workers. About 4.9 million barrels of oil spilled before the well was sealed, damaging fishing, tourism and wildlife along the US Gulf coast.

factCards.term: Fracking: two concerns, and Ireland's response
factCards.definition: Hydraulic fracturing of shale releases gas, but raises concerns over groundwater pollution and induced earthquakes. Ireland banned onshore fracking by law in 2017.

factCards.term: Oil and gas: positive and negative impacts
factCards.definition: Positive: energy supply and security, revenue, jobs. Negative: oil spills; damage to marine life and fishing; conflict with local communities; burning fossil fuels returns stored carbon to the atmosphere, adding to climate change.

factCards.term: Geothermal energy: where the heat comes from and where it is greatest
factCards.definition: Heat comes from the earth's interior, from radioactive decay and residual heat; temperature rises with depth by about 25 to 30 °C per kilometre. Heat is greatest near plate boundaries and hotspots, where magma lies close to the surface.

factCards.term: High-temperature geothermal plant: how it works, in stages
factCards.definition: Groundwater is heated by hot rock near magma; production wells bring steam and hot water to the surface; steam drives turbines to generate electricity and hot water heats buildings (district heating); cooled water is pumped back down a reinjection well.

factCards.term: Iceland: why it has geothermal energy and how it uses it
factCards.definition: On the Mid-Atlantic Ridge above a hotspot. About 9 out of 10 homes use geothermal heat; it gives a quarter to a third of the electricity. Hellisheiði is the largest power station; Reykjavík has district heating; the Blue Lagoon uses Svartsengi's waste water.

factCards.term: Larderello and Wairakei: why each is significant
factCards.definition: Larderello, Tuscany, Italy: the world's first geothermal electricity (1904) and first commercial geothermal power station (1913). Wairakei, New Zealand: a geothermal power station opened in 1958.

factCards.term: Geothermal energy in Ireland: its potential and main use
factCards.definition: Ireland is far from a plate boundary, so it has only low-temperature potential; warm springs at Mallow, Co. Cork, show heated groundwater exists. Ground-source heat pumps, using the steady warmth of shallow ground, are the main use.

factCards.term: Geothermal energy: advantages and disadvantages
factCards.definition: Advantages: renewable, low carbon, reliable, cheap once built. Disadvantages: few suitable places; costly drilling; hydrogen sulphide smell; minerals clog pipes; induced earthquakes, e.g. Basel, Switzerland (2006), where an enhanced project was abandoned.

questions.prompt: Examine how humans interact with the rock cycle, with reference to mining.
questions.model: Mining removes metal ores, coal and salt from the crust, and so acts as a human form of erosion. Ore bodies form where minerals are concentrated by igneous activity or by hot fluids moving through rock. Exploration uses geological surveys and test drilling. Where ore lies near the surface, open-pit mining removes the overburden; where it lies deep, underground shaft mining reaches it through shafts and tunnels. Processing crushes and grinds the ore and separates the mineral from the waste rock. Waste rock is stored in spoil heaps and fine tailings in tailings ponds. Tara Mines, Navan, Co. Meath, is an underground zinc and lead mine, Europe's largest zinc mine, opened in 1977 (production paused from July 2023, restarted at the end of 2024); the ore lies in Carboniferous limestone. Impacts include landscape scars and subsidence, spoil heaps and tailings that take up land, and acid mine drainage: at Avoca, Co. Wicklow, centuries of copper mining left acid drainage that polluted the Avoca River. Dust, noise and heavy traffic affect nearby people. Positive impacts are jobs, exports and local spending. Management includes environmental licensing and monitoring, lined and capped tailings ponds, and rehabilitation after closure, as at Lisheen, Co. Tipperary, which closed in 2015. Internationally, Bingham Canyon, Utah, USA, is one of the largest open-pit mines in the world. The Aberfan disaster in south Wales on 21 October 1966 shows the danger of mining waste: a colliery spoil tip built over springs collapsed into the village after heavy rain, killing 144 people, 116 of them children.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain how humans interact with the rock cycle, with reference to geothermal energy production.
questions.model: Geothermal energy is heat from the earth's interior, produced by radioactive decay and residual heat. Temperature rises with depth at about 25 to 30 °C per kilometre, the geothermal gradient, so the heat is greatest near plate boundaries and hotspots, where magma lies close to the surface. In a high-temperature system, groundwater is heated by hot rock near magma; production wells bring steam and hot water to the surface. Steam drives turbines to generate electricity, hot water heats buildings through district heating, and the cooled water is pumped back down a reinjection well. Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge above a hotspot. About 9 out of 10 homes are heated by geothermal water, and geothermal power provides between a quarter and a third of its electricity; Hellisheiði is its largest geothermal power station, and Reykjavík has a geothermal district heating system. Low-temperature systems use ground-source heat pumps to draw the steady warmth of shallow ground, the type suited to Ireland, which is far from a plate boundary; warm springs at Mallow, Co. Cork, show that heated groundwater exists. Enhanced geothermal systems pump water into hot dry rock to fracture it. Advantages are that geothermal energy is renewable, low in carbon emissions, reliable because it does not depend on the weather, and cheap to run once built. Disadvantages are that it is limited to suitable locations, drilling is expensive, hydrogen sulphide gas causes a rotten-egg smell, minerals are deposited in pipes, and enhanced projects can cause induced earthquakes, as at Basel, Switzerland, in 2006.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain how humans interact with the rock cycle with reference to oil/gas exploitation.
questions.model: Oil and gas form from the remains of tiny marine organisms buried in sea-floor sediment; heat and pressure over millions of years turn them into oil and gas. The hydrocarbons migrate upward through porous, permeable reservoir rock such as sandstone until they are trapped beneath impermeable cap rock such as shale, in an anticline, a fault or a salt dome. Exploitation begins with seismic surveys to locate traps and exploratory wells to test them. Production uses platforms or subsea wells, with pipelines to an onshore terminal. Kinsale Head gas field, off the Co. Cork coast, was discovered in 1971 and produced from 1978; it was Ireland's first commercial gas field and ended in 2020 when it was depleted. The Corrib gas field, off north-west Co. Mayo, was discovered in 1996 and gas first flowed in December 2015; the gas is piped ashore to a processing terminal at Bellanaboy, Co. Mayo. Local opposition, led by the Shell to Sea campaign, objected to a high-pressure raw-gas pipeline near homes, and the Rossport Five were jailed in 2005. Internationally, the Deepwater Horizon rig in the Gulf of Mexico exploded on 20 April 2010, killing 11 workers, and about 4.9 million barrels of oil spilled before the well was sealed, damaging fishing, tourism and wildlife on the US Gulf coast. Positive impacts are energy supply and security, revenue and jobs. Negative impacts are oil spills, damage to marine life and fishing, conflict with local communities, and climate change caused by burning fossil fuels, which returns stored carbon to the atmosphere. Hydraulic fracturing of shale raises concerns about groundwater pollution and induced earthquakes, and Ireland banned onshore fracking by law in 2017.
